messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a 58-year-old South Asian man, had spent his career as a bomb disposal technician, a job that required precision and calm under pressure. However, it wasn't an explosion or a near-miss that brought him to therapy – it was the memory of his young daughter's life-threatening illness several years ago. Rohan recalled the hospital's antiseptic smell, which still made him queasy to this day. Even the sight of medical equipment like needles and drips would transport him back to those anxious days. When Rohan found himself in a situation that triggered these memories – such as being around children or catching a whiff of that distinct hospital scent – he would become hypervigilant, his senses on high alert. His body would tense up, and his mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios. He couldn't shake the feeling that something terrible was lurking just beneath the surface, waiting to pounce. This state of heightened arousal made it impossible for him to fall asleep at night; he needed to stay alert, just in case. These physical reactions were so intense that Rohan began to wonder if he was losing his grip on reality. He felt weak and helpless, unable to protect himself or those he loved from the dangers that seemed to lurk around every corner. The memories of his daughter's illness would come flooding back without warning, triggered by something as mundane as a hospital smell or the sight of medical equipment. When this happened, Rohan would relive the experience in vivid detail – the beeping machines, the antiseptic tang, the desperate feeling of being unable to do anything to help. As these memories resurfaced, Rohan's negative appraisals of himself grew stronger. He believed that he was a weak person, incapable of coping with stress or protecting those around him. This fear of going crazy – of losing control completely – only added to his sense of helplessness. The more he struggled to push these thoughts away, the more they seemed to cling to him. Rohan's work as a bomb disposal technician began to suffer as well. He found himself avoiding situations that might trigger these memories or emotions, opting instead for safer, less demanding tasks. His relationships with his colleagues and family members also started to fray; he became withdrawn and isolated, unable to shake the feeling that he was a burden to those around him. One day, while working on a particularly difficult disposal operation, Rohan caught a whiff of something that smelled eerily like hospital antiseptic. Suddenly, he was back in that hospital room, reliving the terror and helplessness all over again. His body tensed up, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios – and in that moment, Rohan knew he needed help. As he sat in therapy for the first time, Rohan's eyes darted around the room, searching for potential threats or triggers. He fidgeted with his hands, his body still on high alert from years of sleepless nights and hypervigilance. But as he began to talk about his experiences – about the memories that haunted him and the fears that gripped him – Rohan started to realize that he wasn't alone in this fight. He was taking the first tentative steps towards confronting those negative appraisals, towards relearning how to live with himself and his memories. And though it wouldn't be easy, Rohan knew that he had to try – for himself, and for those around him who cared about him most.
